activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
story:
The bus smelled like sunscreen and pine air freshener, and Cooper had been riding it for two hours with his duffel wedged under his knees because the overhead rack was full. He had wanted to stay home. That was the truth he hadn't told his dad, who had been so cheerful at the curb that morning it was almost bizarre, like he was the one getting shipped off for a month. Cooper's actual motivation for going was simpler and more embarrassing: Maya Delgado from his science class had said camp was where she'd learned to find her way around the night sky, and he wanted to be able to do that too.

The boy across the aisle, a wiry kid named Theo who talked with his whole face, leaned over. "You nervous? You look nervous."

"I'm fine," Cooper said, which was mostly a lie. He was fine about the ropes course and the lake. What worried him was the dark, specifically being the only one awake in a cabin full of strangers and not knowing which way anything was.

The first night, after lights out, Theo nudged him and they snuck down to the dock with two other boys, Asher and Ravi. Asher held up his phone, then made an angry sound. "No bars. No compass, no nothing."

"So we point north using the stars," Theo said, squinting up. "That's a thing people do."

"Which stars?" Ravi asked. "There are approximately a billion of them."

Cooper lay back on the warm boards and found the Big Dipper almost immediately, the shape Maya had traced on the classroom window with her finger in April. He remembered her saying something about it, and the memory came back in pieces, the way a photo develops. He found the bowl, then the two stars on its outer edge, and drew a line in his mind, stretching them upward and away.

"I think those two stars point to the North Star," he said slowly. "The ones on the outside of the bowl. They call them the pointer stars."

"You think, or you know?" Theo asked.

Cooper followed the line and there it was, a modest, steady star that didn't look special until you reached it. "That one. That's got to be it."

Asher held his dead phone flat and spun it like a compass card until its top edge lined up with the star. "So that's north. Congratulations, we're officially not lost."

Then Theo laughed, a strange held-in kind of laugh, and pulled a real compass from his sock. "My grandpa made me swear I'd carry it. I've had it the whole time."

Ravi stared at him. "The entire bus ride? The entire hour of us being dramatic about no signal?"

"Your motivations for not mentioning it remain unclear," Cooper said, and everyone groaned at him.

Theo flicked the compass open. The needle swung, shivered, and settled.

It pointed straight at Cooper's star.

story:
The projector hummed while Mr. Reyes took attendance, and Jacob slid into his seat at the back computer lab station, opening the message app before the teacher even finished calling names. He wanted one thing this morning: to find out who had leaked his photo. Two weeks ago he had posted a picture of himself at the hospital, right after his brother's surgery, with a caption about being scared. His account was private. Yet yesterday a kid from another school, someone Jacob had never met, had walked past him at the mall and said, "Hope your brother's okay." His brother was fine. Jacob was not.

He started with his follower list. Eighty-three names. He scrolled slowly, tapping each profile, looking for anyone who might have passed the picture along. Most were kids from his grade. A few were cousins. Then he found one he barely recognized: Derek, a boy from his old elementary school who had followed him three years ago, back when Jacob accepted almost anyone. Derek's page was public, and near the top, Jacob found it. His hospital photo, reposted without the caption, with a joke attached. The room noise, keyboards and chairs and someone's sneaker squeaking, seemed to drop away.

Jacob tested the idea forming in his head. He created a second account under a fake name and tried to view his own page. Nothing. The private setting held, and he could see nothing at all. So the leak had not come from the outside. It had to be someone already inside. He tried once more with a third fake account, just to be sure, and again the wall held. The only people who could have seen the photo were the followers he had already accepted. Derek fit, and Derek's repost fit too.

He walked over to Marisol's station, because she had been friends with Derek's younger sister. "Can you message him for me?" he asked. "Tell him to take it down."

Marisol pulled off one earbud. She had her own project on screen, a photography portfolio she'd been building all semester for the district contest. "Why should I? Derek's been trying to get views all month. He'll listen if it helps him, not if it helps you."

"Tell him I'll give him credit if he ever wants to use one of my brother's drawings. Or tell him everyone at school will think he reposts old stuff because he can't make anything new." Jacob watched her weigh it, watched her lens of attention shift from her portfolio to him. "It's not trivial to me," he added. "That photo was just for people I know."

Marisol sent the message. In five minutes, Derek replied: the post was gone. But when Jacob checked his follower list again, he understood the other half of it. He removed Derek, and then he kept going, tapping remove on name after name, kids from elementary school, strangers, people whose faces no longer coincided with anyone he actually talked to. The list shrank from eighty-three to thirty-one.

Mr. Reyes called for attention, and Jacob closed the app. On Marisol's screen, her contest portfolio glowed, and she was still smiling at her own good news. "Thirty-one," Jacob said quietly, counting what was left of the list he used to brag about.

"It'll grow again," Marisol said. "Only slower this time."

He looked at the empty seat where the projector light fell, then logged off the computer entirely.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
story:
Grayson's sneakers squeaked on the gym floor as he lined up with fourteen other boys for the last day of basketball tryouts. His friend Priya sat on the bleachers with a stopwatch, waiting for her turn to help Coach Herrera record sprints. She was only there because she had missed the swim team cutoff by half a second, and she hadn't wanted to go home and stare at the notice on her fridge.

"She said my time didn't make the top eight," Priya said quietly while the coach set up cones. "But I swam the hundred in Texas this summer, and I was faster than that. I got slower. That's what doesn't make sense."

Grayson took a drink from his water bottle and thought about it while he jogged in place. He had seen Priya race in the summer too, at the big aquatic center where her club practiced. Their school's own pool was so short that when he counted the lane ropes, you touched the wall almost before you got going. If the Texas pool was longer, then swimming the same distance there would mean fewer turns, and fewer turns meant you couldn't push off and glide the way you could at school.

"Wait," he said. "Was the Texas pool the big one? The fifty-meter one?"

Priya nodded. "Long course. That's what it's called. Our pool is short course, twenty-five yards." She turned the stopwatch over in her hands. "Coach Benson said her club times can't be compared directly with her tryout times. That's why I had to swim again here."

Grayson chewed on that. So Priya hadn't gotten slower at all. Her tryout time just couldn't be stacked against summer races, because the pools weren't the same distance end to end, and the cutoff list had been built from numbers that didn't match. His mind drifted to the previous spring, when he had quit track after one bad meet and told himself he was simply not a runner. He wondered now whether he had quit over one false measurement too.

"Go!" Coach Herrera shouted, and Grayson burst down the court. His legs were heavy from two days of drills, and fatigue hindered his footwork on the crossover, but he forced himself to keep his eyes up and find the open teammate. The ball left his fingers and dropped through the net without touching the rim.

After the drill, he jogged back to Priya. "Tell Coach Benson you want to swim the hundred again," he said. "Or ask her to convert your long course time. You're not slower. You were just measured in a different pool."

Priya looked at the list of names the coach had started writing on his clipboard, then at the gym doors. "I almost didn't come today," she said. "I thought it was permanent, that cut."

"It's not," Grayson said. He picked up his ball and squared his shoulders toward the hoop. "Nothing's permanent until the roster goes up on that door."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
story:
The fruit fly problem started at Avery's kitchen table, where her little brother Dex had left a bruised peach in a bowl for two weeks. "Fruit makes them," Dex insisted, pointing at the tiny flies circling the bowl. "The peach grows them by itself." Avery had her doubts, but she had no proof, and Monday's science class gave her an idea for getting some.

Mr. Okafor's room smelled like pencil shavings and the rubber gaskets from the sink sprayers. At the front counter sat a stack of clean jars, a square of wire gauze, and two slabs of raw meat wrapped in paper. The lab sheets were blank except for one line: a question about where maggots come from. Avery raised her hand before anyone else could. "My brother says rotten food makes flies by itself. Can we settle it?"

"Then formulate a guess we can test," Mr. Okafor said. "Something the jars can confirm or knock down." Avery wrote her guess at the top of her sheet: flies come from outside, from other flies, not from the meat. If she was wrong, the jars would show it either way, which was the whole point of setting them up.

Her group put meat in four jars and left two of them open. They stretched gauze over the mouths of the other two and wound string around the rims so nothing could crawl in. Avery pressed her eye to the mesh on the covered jars. She could see the meat clearly, gray and glistening, but the gauze kept anything the size of a fly from reaching it. "Same meat, same shelf, same air," she said. "The only difference is the cover." By Wednesday, white specks no bigger than grains of rice had appeared along the edges of the meat in the open jars. By Friday, the specks had become maggots, and flies had found the open jars too, landing and lifting off again like they owned them. The covered jars sat clean. Nothing grew on that meat at all.

"Look," said her lab partner Naomi, holding up both lab sheets. "Open jars, maggots. Gauze jars, nothing." Avery turned to the history poster on the back wall, the one with the timeline of scientists, and stopped at a name she had walked past a hundred times without reading. "Francesco Redi," she said slowly. "1668. He put meat in jars, and maggots grew in the open jars, but not in the jars covered with gauze that kept flies off the meat." She had done his exact experiment without knowing it, and his result matched hers jar for jar. "That's like testimony," Naomi said. "Somebody tested the same guess three hundred fifty years before us and got the same answer."

At home, Avery carried the peach bowl to the back porch and set it on the railing. Dex watched from the door. "You're letting them out?" he asked. "No," Avery said. "I'm letting you watch." She pointed at the peach, where a fruit fly was landing on the bruised spot, and Dex leaned in close, his nose almost touching the bowl.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
story:
The cafeteria had a new poster by the milk line: JOIN THE MILLIONS WHO ALREADY SWITCHED TO VOLT SODA. Alice stopped in front of it with her tray, because beneath the giant smiling face of the pop star Dree Santino, there was nothing else. No flavor, no price, no reason at all.

"Millions," said Priya, reading over her shoulder. "That's a lot of people."

Alice frowned. "Switched to it from what? And why?" The poster didn't say. It just assumed that if everyone was drinking Volt, you would want to drink Volt too, so you wouldn't be the one person standing outside the crowd. She thought about that all through lunch, turning her carton of plain milk over in her hands like it might hold an answer.

After school, media club met in the library, and Mr. Okafor had put out stacks of magazines for their ad-cutting project. Alice flipped through them with Priya and Marcus, hunting for examples. "Look at this one," Marcus said, holding up a page. "Nine out of ten teens choose Fizz Blast." Priya found another: "Don't be the last one on your block without a Snack Rocket." It was the same trick over and over, and once Alice saw the pattern, she couldn't stop seeing it, like when you learn a word and suddenly it's everywhere.

"It's called a bandwagon appeal," Alice said, reading from a list of techniques on Mr. Okafor's handout. "It urges you to do something because everyone else is doing it. It never tells you what the thing actually does better." She tapped the Volt poster she'd sketched into her notebook. "The Dree Santino part is a celebrity testimonial too. He's probably paid to smile like that."

"Maybe," Marcus said. "But Dree is genuinely good. I'd still buy it."

For the club's bulletin board, Alice made her own counter-poster: VOLT SODA. WHAT DOES IT DO BETTER? NOTHING ON THE POSTER SAYS. She pinned it up in the hallway on Friday morning, feeling proud. By afternoon, someone had drawn a mustache on Dree's face on the original poster and written VOLT TASTES LIKE BATTERY ACID underneath, which was not what she'd meant at all. Mr. Okafor took both posters down and told her the hallway wasn't the place for unapproved materials, even clever ones.

Still, on the bus home, Priya slid into the seat beside her. "I asked my brother what Volt actually does better," she said. "He said nothing, it's just soda. Then he asked for a sip of my water." Alice laughed, but she kept looking out the window at the billboard of Dree's enormous smile going by, still promising millions, still selling nothing.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
story:
Blake had saved twenty-two dollars from mowing lawns, and he intended to spend every cent on the one thing he had wanted since March: a plush shark from the kiosk near the food court. He walked past the transparent glass of the aquarium store, where a wall of fish tanks emitted a soft blue glow, and smelled popcorn and soy sauce drifting from the food court. Then he saw the kiosk, and he saw the price sign, and his stomach dropped. The shark, which had cost eighteen dollars in April, was now thirty-five. A line of six kids stretched from the counter toward the pretzel stand.

"You're kidding," Blake said to the kiosk owner, a woman with gray braids.

"Everyone wants them since that video," she said. "I only get ten a week from my supplier. When I run out, people offer me more than the sticker price just to hold the next one."

Blake walked away with his money still folded in his pocket. At the far end of the food court, farmers had set up long tables for a weekend market inside the mall, which happened once a month. He drifted toward it because it was quieter there, and because a crate of strawberries caught his eye. A hand-lettered sign read: Two baskets for four dollars. He blinked. In April, at the market by his grandmother's house, one small basket had cost four dollars.

He picked up a basket and turned it over. The berries were dark red all the way to the stem, and the whole table smelled sweet, like jam before it cooked. Behind the strawberries, a fish farmer was laying out salmon on ice, and Blake overheard him tell a customer, "It comes from the estuary, where the river meets the sound, so it's fresh as anything."

"Why so cheap now?" Blake asked the strawberry farmer, a man with dirt still under his fingernails. "These were double the price last month."

"It's the peak of the local harvest," the farmer said. "I've got more than I can pick."

Blake stood there holding his basket, and an idea began to form, quiet and slow, the way the light from the tanks had glowed. Six kids had lined up for ten plush sharks. Here, a whole table sagged under more strawberries than the farmer could pick. Scarce and wanted meant expensive. Plentiful meant cheap. He wanted to see if the idea held somewhere else, so he walked back toward the pretzel stand, where a vendor was throwing away a tray of day-old cinnamon twists. "A dollar each," the vendor called to anyone passing. "Way less than lunchtime, before they ran out by one o'clock." An hour ago, Blake remembered, that same tray had emptied fast at full price.

He carried his two baskets of strawberries to a table by the tanks, where his friend Marisol was doing homework. He set one basket in front of her.

"Those cost four dollars?" she said. "For both?"

"Peak harvest," Blake said, and ate a strawberry, which was warm from sitting in the sun of the skylight, and so sweet he closed his eyes for a second.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Arthur slid the chicken breasts out of the refrigerator and lined them up on the counter like pale little pillows. Family dinner night had been his idea this semester, ever since his grandmother announced she would retire from cooking the Sunday meal and hand the job to whoever wanted it. His sister wanted takeout. Arthur wanted to cook it himself, in the school's kitchen classroom, where the ovens actually worked and there were drawers full of real tools.

He found the tool he wanted right away: a digital thermometer with a thin metal probe. His grandmother had always judged chicken by slicing it open and checking that the juices ran clear and the meat looked white. But Arthur had read the guidelines taped inside the cabinet door, and he kept turning one line over in his mind: U.S. food safety guidelines say poultry is safely cooked when its thickest part reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, or about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer. Not color. Not juices. A number, checked in the thickest part. Could the outside look done while the inside was still dangerous? He wanted to find out.

He set the oven, laid the chicken in a baking dish, and slid it in. While it cooked, his classmate Marisol came over to watch. "My mom just pokes it with a fork," she said.

"That's guessing," Arthur said. "The thermometer measures the actual temperature in the middle. That's where the chicken is thickest, so that's where you check." He tapped the cabinet card. "It has to reach 165 degrees Fahrenheit, which is about 74 degrees Celsius."

He was hesitant at first about where to stick the probe, worried he would hit the pan and get a false reading. So he tried a small experiment. He slid the probe into the side of one breast, angling it toward the center of the thickest part, and watched the numbers climb: 130, 148, 157. He pulled it out, wiped it, and tested a second breast, then a third. They read 160, 155, and 161. Same oven, same pan, different temperatures. The pieces weren't cooking evenly, and guessing by color would never have caught that.

He slid the pan back in for five more minutes and tested again. This time all three probes settled at 165 or higher, and the smallest one read 170. He wondered whether the big pieces had hidden cold spots too, so he checked each one twice, in different spots, like a doctor double-checking a diagnosis before telling anyone the news. Every reading held.

At home that evening, his family gathered around the table. His grandmother cut into her chicken, looked at the white meat, and raised an eyebrow at him.

"Tested it three ways," Arthur said, and set the thermometer down beside her plate. "It hit 165 in the thickest part. You can check."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The candle flames fluctuated every time Isaac's little sister, Prue, breathed, which she was doing on purpose. "Stop huffing at the candles," he said. "The power's already out. You don't have to blow out the rest of it."

"I'm not huffing. I'm sighing. It's different." She sighed again, and two flames wobbled in agreement.

Isaac leaned back on the couch and thought about why the whole street had gone dark at exactly 7:04. It hadn't flickered or faltered the way it did in ordinary storms, dropping out in stages as the voltage seemed to fluctuate before failing. This had been one clean cut, every house at once, like someone had snipped a single thread. A single thread meant a single point of failure somewhere near the top of the street. He had a guess about exactly where.

"That face you're making," Prue said, "is your detective face. It's not robust enough for a real mystery. You look like a kid who lost a sock."

"It's not a sock." He got up, took the flashlight from the drawer, and angled it out the front window. Halfway up the block, right where the big oak leaned over the road, something thin and black lay draped across the sidewalk. He felt a cold little jolt in his stomach. He and his friend Marcus had walked under that oak at 6:50, fourteen minutes before the lights died.

"Stay here," he told Prue, and he went out the front door and stood at the edge of the porch, well back from the sidewalk, and called Marcus.

"You seeing what I'm seeing?" Marcus answered on the second ring.

"The wire across the walk. Marcus, we walked right past that spot before the lights went out."

"So it fell after us. Lucky us. I already told my dad and he called it in. He says a fallen line can still be deadly even when it's not sparking. Treat it as live, stay well away, get it reported." A pause. "Which we did. So technically I solved the mystery before you even made your detective face."

"You can't see my face over the phone."

"I can hear it. It's not robust."

When the utility truck finally came, its amber lights sweeping the candles in the living room into a slow gold tide, Prue tugged Isaac's sleeve. "So the wire was the whole problem? One wire?"

"One wire that looked dead and wasn't taking any chances," Isaac said. "Some things you don't poke to find out."

"Like you," said Prue, and huffed out a candle.

story:
Madison wanted one thing before lunch: to post the selfie she had taken on her front porch that morning, the one where her new braces made her grin look lopsided in a way she actually liked. She sat down at the computer lab's last open machine, opened her photo folder, and got the picture on screen. Behind her shoulder, blurry but there, stood the blue mailbox at the end of her driveway.

"You going to post that?" Deshawn asked from the next seat, spinning his chair around.

"After I check it," Madison said. She zoomed in on the background. On the porch railing, plain as anything, sat the little metal numbers her dad had screwed in when they moved in. 314. Behind those, at the curb, the green street sign read ELMONT ST. She sat back. She had learned the hard way, from a cyber safety assembly video two weeks ago, that a stranger could work out where a photo was taken from exactly this kind of thing, a street sign, a house number, even a school logo on a shirt.

She opened the image editor and cropped the picture tight around her face. The railing, the numbers, the sign all dropped away, and the photo transformed into something she felt okay about. Then she tested her idea the way the video had suggested. She picked a random picture from the class trip album on the shared drive, a group shot outside the science museum, and zoomed in. There in the corner was the museum's banner with its address printed along the bottom. Anyone looking at that picture could figure out where forty kids from her school had been standing on a Tuesday morning. She deleted her copy of the album and messaged Priya, who had taken it, to do the same.

"That's the whole mechanism," Madison said to Deshawn, pointing at the banner on screen. "It's not some invisible tracking thing. It's just stuff in the background."

Deshawn leaned over and looked for a long moment. "Huh," he said. He pulled out his phone, found the selfie he'd posted that morning, and stared at it. In the background, over his shoulder, his little brother stood grinning in front of their front door, wearing his soccer jersey with the Riverside Middle bobcat stretched across the chest.

"Take it down?" Madison asked.

"Already did," Deshawn said, still tapping. He held up the phone to show her the delete confirmation, and behind it, on his screen, sat a comment from an account with no picture and a name she'd never seen: "Nice house on 314 Elmont, by the way."

activity: going to a first school dance
story:
Hannah stood at the edge of the gymnasium in her one nice dress and watched the fog machine do its work under the basketball hoop. The thermostat on the wall said the custodian had lost some kind of war, because the room was freezing and half the dance committee was huddled near the speakers like penguins. She had wanted to come to this dance for one reason: Priya was going to be there, and Hannah had spent two weeks deciding whether to say anything about that, and had settled on the brave strategy of standing near the punch table and hoping fate would handle it.

Fate, so far, had handled nothing.

Then Marcus appeared at the door with a box of glow stick bracelets for the seventh graders, and one of them wasn't working. He snapped it, shook it, held it to the light like it owed him money. "Where's the light even coming from in these?" he said. "There's no battery."

"Maybe you cracked it wrong," said his friend Dominic.

Hannah took the bracelet and turned it over. She bent it slowly and felt, inside the plastic, a tiny stiff thing give way with a click, like a small bone. The tube lit up green along half its length. She bent the dark half the same careful way and felt a second click, and the whole bracelet glowed.

"There's a little glass vial inside," she said. "Bending breaks it."

"That's it?" said Marcus.

"And the vial has hydrogen peroxide in it. When it breaks, it mixes with other chemicals and a dye that are in the rest of the tube. That's the light."

"Does that have a name?" Dominic asked. "It feels like it has a name."

"It's called chemiluminescence," Hannah said. "My cousin worked at a party supply store and said it about forty times."

Marcus began snapping bracelets with scientific interest, and the sound began to irritate Ms. Reyes, who was guarding the door, because every seventh grader in a ten-foot radius now wanted one and the box was not infinite. Hannah flexed the bracelet onto her wrist and noticed Priya had drifted over to watch the snapping.

"You broke it and it got better," Priya said.

"Only works once," Hannah said. "Then you just have to enjoy the glow while it lasts."

Priya held out her wrist, the unbroken bracelet dangling. "Show me?"

Hannah clicked it green, and the two of them walked out onto the floor under the hoop, where the fog was finally doing something beautiful.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
story:
The food bank shared a parking lot with the seniors' residence, so Gavin's mom dropped him at the front door of the residence first, where a volunteer named Dora was pushing a cart of grocery boxes down the hallway. "You must be the new helper," she said. "We're doing deliveries today. Some of the folks here can't carry a box up the stairs, so we bring it to them."

Gavin took half the stack and followed her. He had expected the food bank to be a warehouse with long lines, and he'd pictured something quieter too, a building full of people who never spoke. That second picture fell apart at the second door, where Mr. Hall greeted them with a joke about the elevator being slower than his old tractor.

At the fourth door, a woman named Mrs. Okafor counted the cans in her box twice. "Tuna, beans, rice, peaches," she said. "Same as last month. And the month before." She didn't sound ungrateful, but she didn't sound happy either. On the walk back, Gavin noticed she was the only one who had counted.

He wondered about that the whole afternoon. Maybe she was worried the supply was running low, or maybe she was checking whether anyone had taken something out. He couldn't see the reason directly, so he tested a simple idea: he asked Dora what Mrs. Okafor liked to cook. "Soups," Dora said. "But she never says so, because she thinks complaining about a free box sounds rude."

The next week, Gavin slipped a note into the signup sheet the food bank used for donations, marking Mrs. Okafor's building for a soup drive. When the boxes went out again, hers held broth and barley and a bag of dried lentils. She counted the cans as usual, then stopped at the lentils and smiled at them for a long moment. "Well," she said. "Somebody was paying attention."

In the hallway afterward, Mrs. Okafor caught up with them. "Can I ask you something, dear? How long have food banks existed in this country? I came here in the seventies, and I don't remember any." Gavin had looked this up at the library only the day before, hoping someone would ask. "Canada's first food bank opened in 1981," he said, "in Edmonton, Alberta." She repeated the words like she was tasting them. "Eighty-one. I'd been here ten years by then."

The following Tuesday, Mrs. Okafor was waiting by the door with a pot of lentil soup, enough for the whole hallway. Mr. Hall brought spoons from his room. Gavin carried the pot carefully to the common room, both hands steady, and set it in the middle of the table.

story:
Mrs. Ortega had said little Sophie would be asleep by eight, and she was, so Megan stood alone in the lamplit living room with forty minutes of quiet and her phone at nine percent. She was supposed to be reading for English, and instead she was doing what she always did in a strange house: looking at everything.

The coffee table held a mug of cold tea, a scatter of mail, and a bottle of children's vitamins, orange and shaped like bears, sitting right at toddler height. Megan remembered her mother dragging a chair to the pantry one afternoon, muttering that medicines and cleaning products belong up high and out of reach, because little kids explore by putting things in their mouths. Megan had rolled her eyes at the time, thirteen and full of small rebellions, and had not helped move the bottles. She picked up the vitamins now and looked around the room. Under the sink she found dish soap and a spray bottle of cleaner, crouched there like they were hiding. She carried everything to the highest kitchen shelf, the one perpendicular to the doorway where Sophie could not see it even if she stood on a chair. Then she sat back down, feeling both pleased and slightly ridiculous, since Sophie was asleep and would probably stay asleep.

Twenty minutes later Sophie appeared in the hallway, barefoot and wailing, and Megan's ridiculous feeling evaporated. She scooped the girl up, found the sippy cup, and walked her slowly around the living room to settle her. Sophie stopped crying almost at once. Then she leaned over Megan's arm and reached, with the calm certainty of someone who knew exactly what she wanted, toward the empty spot on the coffee table where the vitamins used to be. She opened her mouth and made a little chomping motion, like a goldfish.

"So that's where they always are," Megan whispered. Her whole body went cold and then hot. She had moved the vitamins because of something her mother once said, without really believing it mattered, and now the proof was dangling from her arms, smacking her lips at a bare patch of wood. Sophie had been sneaking bears off that table all along, quietly, whenever someone left them out. Probably not enough to hurt her. Probably. Megan made a note to tell Mrs. Ortega exactly where the bottle had been sitting, and how many might be missing, even if it meant admitting she had gone through the cupboards.

She rocked Sophie until the girl's eyes closed, then lowered her into the crib with the care of someone defusing a bomb. When Mrs. Ortega's headlights swept the window, Megan was sitting on the couch with her English book open, though she had read the same page three times.

"Everything okay?" Mrs. Ortega asked, keys still in her hand.

"Mostly," Megan said. "But we should talk about the vitamins."

Mrs. Ortega's eyes went straight to the empty coffee table, and she said, "Oh no. Not again."

story:
Alexa needed the green pen. Mr. Okafor had promised the two students who wrote the most accurate product reviews for the class energy-unit project a chance to test the new solar panels after school, and Alexa had wanted to touch those panels since September. The problem was the worksheet, which asked them to sort sentences from real reviews into two piles: facts you could check, and everything else. She had underlined half of her review and could not say why.

Beside her, Marcus was already on his third review, tapping his pencil like a drummer. "This one's easy," he whispered. "It says the hand-crank flashlight is the best on the market. Best. That's just somebody talking." He moved on before Alexa could ask how he knew.

Alexa stared at her own page. The rechargeable battery pack review said the design was beautiful, the instructions were boring, and the company should include a spare cord. Beautiful. Boring. Should. She said the words under her breath and felt something click, the way it did when a graph finally showed its pattern. Those words were judgments. You could not check them the way you could check "the battery holds 2,000 milliamp hours" or "the cord is one meter long." If a sentence leaned on best, worst, beautiful, boring, or should, it was almost always someone's opinion dressed up as information. "Judgment words," she murmured, and circled every one.

She started generating sentences to test the idea, one plain fact and one judgment word, over and over, like mixing chemicals to see which combination reacted. "The fan runs at two speeds" went in the check pile. "The fan is the worst gift ever" went in the other. It worked every time. She raised her hand so fast her chair squeaked, and when Mr. Okafor called on her, she laid out her rule in forty seconds flat. He asked her to write it on the board for the class vote, since they graded each other's projects by simple democracy, hands up, majority rules.

The vote was close. Marcus got the second panel slot by one hand, and it was Alexa's own friend Priya who raised it, because Priya's review was the one Alexa had gently pulled apart in front of everyone, all those shoulds and bests laid bare on the overhead projector. Priya had laughed, but not really.

At three o'clock Alexa stood at the window watching Marcus clip the panel to its stand outside, his breath fogging the glass. The class had asked to borrow her list of judgment words, and Mr. Okafor had called her method legitimate, which was worth more than a slot on a Wednesday afternoon. Still. She pressed one finger against the cold pane.

"Save me a turn," she called through the crack in the window, and Marcus, without looking up, tilted the panel half a degree toward her.

story:
Samantha adjusted the fine focus knob one hair's width at a time, and the onion skin slide snapped into view like magic. Sort of. The cells looked like pale bricks stacked in rows, and she could see the thick cell walls easily, plus the thin membrane hugging the inside edge. The problem was the nucleus. Her lab sheet had a diagram with an arrow pointing to a dark dot, but her cells showed nothing but faint gray outlines.

Maybe her stain had failed. She had dripped the iodine the way the directions said, but the drop had pooled at the edge of the coverslip instead of soaking through. She peeled off the coverslip, added one smaller drop right onto the tissue, and lowered the glass again slowly so no bubbles would sneak underneath.

"You look intense," said Marcus from the next stool. He was already labeling his drawing, smug about it.

"Can you actually see the nucleus?" Samantha asked.

He leaned back from his eyepiece. "Kind of? A speck. I think."

She returned to her microscope. This time, in three cells near the center, dark little spots floated inside the gray. That was it. She drew the cells on her sheet, careful to coordinate the arrows on her diagram with what she actually saw, and not with the printed example. She wrote cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus.

Then she stopped, pencil hovering. "Who figured out that dot was a thing? Somebody had to be the first person to look and say, there's a spot."

Marcus shrugged, but Priya across the table said, "I read about it in a weird old book at my uncle's house. The Scottish botanist Robert Brown described the cell nucleus in 1831 while studying orchid cells." She said it fast, like she was afraid she'd forget a word.

"Orchids," Samantha repeated. "So he saw it in flower cells, not onions."

"Flower cells first. Then it works everywhere."

Samantha tested the idea. There were prepared slides in the wooden box at the front, including one of orchid tissue. If the same dark spot showed up in both the orchid and her onion, then the nucleus wasn't some onion quirk or a mistake in her staining. It was a rule about cells. She carried the orchid slide back, swapped it in, and focused.

Dark spots. Same as hers, just bigger.

"Ha!" She waved Priya over. "Look. Mine and yours match."

Priya bent to the eyepiece and grinned. "You just did what he did, only with two plants."

"Two plants and a lot of iodine," Samantha said.

That evening she wrote her lab report and taped an extra note inside the cover, addressed to her older cousin Elena, who had mailed her the little magnifying glass that started all of it. "Dear Elena," she wrote, "today I saw the same dark dot in onion cells and orchid cells, the one Robert Brown described in 1831. My first slide had no dot at all, so I restained it and it worked. Being a scientist might be feasible after all. Your (possibly future) favorite botanist, Samantha." She drew a tiny cell at the bottom, with three careful labels and an arrow pointing at the dot.

She sealed the envelope and set it on the counter by her lunchbox for morning.

Theodore sat on the counter behind the teller line, next to the staff washing machine, holding his pizza-stained shirt at arm's length. The orange blotch on the chest was from the slice he had eaten in the parking lot an hour ago, and it shone even under the break room's dim fluorescent light. His mother had a double shift at the bank, so she had traded him a deal: learn to do laundry, start to finish, and he could use the machine in the back while she worked the window.

First he took a census of the laundry bag she had left him. He counted six dark items, four whites, and one red sock that he set aside like a suspect, since it looked capable of turning everything pink. He sorted, he loaded, and then, before starting the wash, he tried an experiment. Why not just water? Grease was wet, water was wet. He held the stained corner under the tap and rubbed the fabric against itself with aggressive, determined strokes. The blotch dimmed slightly and then stopped, a pale orange ghost that refused to move.

"Why won't you budge?" he muttered.

Ms. Alvarez, the custodian, came in to empty the trash. "Pizza?" she said, nodding at the shirt. "Water alone won't touch that. Use the detergent."

He acquired the bottle from the supply shelf above the sink and squinted at the back label while she waited. "It says here detergent molecules have one end that's attracted to water and another end that's attracted to oil and grease." He looked up. "So one half of the molecule likes my stain and the other half likes the wash water?"

"Grabby little things," Ms. Alvarez said, and rolled her cart out.

Theodore wondered whether it could really work that way, each molecule reaching out in two directions at once, invisible and busy. He drizzled detergent straight onto the blotch, waited while the sink filled with hot water, and pushed the shirt under. Then he watched. The orange ghost loosened at its edges, feathering out like ink in water, and the fabric beneath came back white, thread by thread. He fished the shirt out, wrung it, and held it to the light. Nothing. The stain had gone wherever the water had gone, carried off by its invisible partners.

He ran the full load after that, sorted and soaped and timed, and when the dryer buzzed he folded everything on the break table, matching socks into pairs. He carried the stack out to the teller line and set his clean shirt on top, stain side up.

His mother glanced over between customers. "You actually did it," she said. "What happened to the pizza?"

"The molecules took it," Theodore said.

story:
Kate had been stuck on the same eight measures for forty minutes, and Mr. Alvarez had stopped counting her mistakes out loud, which was worse than counting them. "Again," he said, and she played it again, and her left hand still fumbled the third note every single time, like a foot catching on a loose stair.

"Enough for today," he finally said. "Same piece Thursday." He closed the lid over the keys, gently, as if the piano were something durable that would outlast both of them. On the drive home Kate sat with her hands in her lap and didn't let her mother console her, even when her mom said maybe the passage was just too hard for now. It wasn't too hard. She could play every note separately. It was only the sequence, the order, that fell apart.

That night she slept nine hours, mostly out of sulking, and in the morning she came downstairs early, made toast she didn't eat, and sat down at the kitchen keyboard just to prove the passage was still broken. Her left hand played all eight measures straight through, clean, twice in a row. She stared at her own fingers like they belonged to somebody else.

She thought back to the summer, when she'd had her vaccine shot and a sore arm and had skipped cello practice for two days, and the day she came back her bowing on the hard etude had been smoother than before she stopped. She'd assumed her teacher had been wrong to call it a coincidence. Now she wasn't sure. The pattern was the same: practice, then sleep, then sudden improvement with no extra practice in between.

So she tested it. She picked a new six-note pattern she had never played, drilled it until she was missing it about half the time, wrote down exactly how many mistakes she made on ten tries, and then refused to touch the keyboard for the rest of the day. Six mistakes out of ten, recorded on a napkin and folded into her pocket. At school she caught herself tapping the pattern on her desk and sat on her hands.

Thursday she got to the studio fifteen minutes early and played the old passage first, to warm up, and to show off a little. It was still clean. Mr. Alvarez raised an eyebrows. "When did you practice this?"

"Monday night. Then not at all. I slept on it." She unfolded the napkin and played her new test pattern ten times, counting under her breath. Three mistakes. "Yesterday it was six."

He leaned on the piano. "Out of ten tries?"

"Out of ten. Same pattern, same hand, no practice since."

He looked at the napkin, then at her. "Do it again," he said. "I want to count."

Charlie carried the sack of flour across the farmers' market like it was a sleeping cat, careful not to jostle it. She had spent her last twelve dollars on it because tonight she was making bread for her family, all by herself, the way Gran used to. At the egg stall she paused to read the note tucked in her pocket again, the one Gran had mailed from the hospital before she got better and moved away to Aunt Ruth's.

"Ten minutes of kneading before it rises," the letter said. "No cheating. The proteins in the flour wake up when they meet water, and kneading makes them stronger and stretchier. That stretch is what holds the bubbles. Love, Gran."

Charlie turned that over as she walked past the tomato pyramid. Invisible stuff inside flour, proteins she would never see, doing work she could only feel. It seemed strange that ten minutes could matter so much, but Gran never put numbers in a letter unless she meant them.

At home, the kitchen went quiet except for the radio. Charlie mixed flour and water, then kneaded for about two minutes until her arms ached, covered the bowl with a towel, and left it. An hour later the dough had risen into a soft, lazy hill. She punched it down, shaped it, slid it into the oven, and waited, remembering how Gran had once caught her skipping the kneading entirely. Charlie had concealed that loaf's failure by blaming the oven, and Gran had let her, which somehow felt worse.

The loaf came out flat and dense, like a brick with delusions. Charlie stood over it, thinking. Same flour, same oven. The difference had to be the kneading, because that was the only thing she'd changed from the loaf that worked last month. If the proteins truly got stronger and stretchier with kneading, then two minutes wasn't enough and ten wasn't a random number. There was a rule in there, invisible, and the flat loaf had just proved it.

She started over. This time she set the timer and kneaded the full ten minutes, feeling the dough change under her hands, going from shaggy to smooth to something that pushed back like it was alive. While she worked, her little brother read the note out loud and asked why the market's bread table had a sign that said "no controversy," and Charlie laughed and said that was about the jam judging last summer, not about flour. The dough rose high and proud, and when the second loaf came out golden, she cut the first slice and handed it to her brother.

"Taste it," she said. "Then tell me if you can feel the difference ten minutes makes."

story:
Nicholas sat on his bedroom floor with his laptop open and a peach juice box beside him, which had cost him his last two dollars because he'd spent his allowance Monday on a flimsy dragon kite he never flew. He'd punched his wall that same afternoon, over a game, and his knuckles still stung. That was the strange part. He hadn't even been that angry a second before his fist moved.

His older sister Priya knocked and came in without waiting, the way she always did. She wanted the desk lamp for her room because hers had burned out, and she'd been leaving sticky notes on his door all week, each one more polite and more pointed than the last.

"You can have it after I finish something," Nicholas said.

"You said that Tuesday." Priya sat on the edge of his bed anyway. "What are you even doing?"

"I'm looking stuff up." He turned the laptop so she could see the page he'd found. His cousin Marcus had told him at Thanksgiving that teenagers basically have unfinished brains, and Nicholas had decided to check it, the way he'd once checked whether Marcus was right about hot water freezing faster than cold. That one had turned out mostly wrong. This one seemed to be true.

"It's called the prefrontal cortex," he read aloud. "The part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses. It keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties."

"So you're not finished," Priya said.

"So I'm not finished." He looked at his sore knuckles, then at the kite still folded in its plastic sleeve in the corner, bought with money meant to last the week. It was almost a relief, like finding out the wobbly shelf had never been screwed in right in the first place. Not an excuse. Just a fact he could now see, even though he couldn't see the thing itself.

He decided to test it. If his planning equipment was still under construction, maybe he could build something outside his head to make up for it, the way you'd put a rail on a staircase. He got a marker and a sticky note and wrote "think two seconds first," and pressed it to the wall above his desk where his fist had landed.

Priya watched him, then pointed at the peach juice box, half drunk and sweating on the carpet. "You spent everything you had on that and the kite."

"It's nectar," Nicholas said. "Peach nectar. That's literally what the box says." He handed it to her so she could see, careful not to spill it, thinking two seconds first as instructed.

She read the ingredients, snorted, and set it down. "You're going to be like this until your twenties?"

"Apparently." He unplugged the lamp and held it out to her. "Bring it back when your new bulb comes."

Priya stood in the doorway with the lamp tucked under her arm, its cord dragging behind her like a tail.

story:
Jade pushed the shopping cart past the cereal aisle with the focus of a general planning an invasion. Tonight was her night to cook, her first real dinner since Mom had started working late, and she had decided on potato soup with a mountain of caramelized onions on top. Her little brother Theo trailed behind her, dropping a box of crackers into the cart whenever she wasn't looking.

"Put those back," Jade said, fishing out the third box.

"You can't abandon a cracker family once you've picked it up," Theo said solemnly, holding two boxes together like they were friends.

She grabbed them from him and put them back, but not before he sprinted toward the produce section with the agile speed of a kid who knew he'd win any race in a grocery store. When she caught up, he was holding an onion in each hand and pretending they were arguing with each other.

"One bag," she said. "We need a lot." She counted out onions, checked the potatoes, and grabbed a lemon, because a recipe she'd read at school claimed lemon made everything better. The soup was technically part of a life-skills unit, though Jade privately thought "curriculum" was a fancy word for "make your kid cook dinner so you don't have to."

At home, the kitchen was hers. She set the cutting board down, peeled the first onion, and started chopping. Halfway through, her eyes began to burn. By the end of the onion, tears were streaming down her face so hard that Theo, who had wandered in to steal crackers, stopped in the doorway.

"Why are you crying?" he demanded. "Did the soup die?"

"It's the onion," Jade said, blinking hard. "I'm not sad, it just, ow." She wiped her eyes and stared at the half-chopped pile. A whole onion had sat on the counter all morning and done nothing. The moment she cut into it, her eyes flooded. So something about cutting it had to release something. She picked up a whole onion and held it right up to her face and sniffed. Nothing. Then she leaned over the chopped pieces and her eyes instantly watered again.

"Ha," she said, pointing at the pile. "Whole onion, no problem. Cut onion, waterworks. Cutting it breaks its cells, and that releases enzymes that make a gas. The gas floats up and gets in your eyes, and your eyes water to fight it off."

"That's the weirdest vegetable fact I've ever heard," Theo said. "Can you fight it?"

Jade considered the problem like a scientist with a knife. If the gas floated upward, maybe her eyes just needed to be out of the line of fire. She chopped the second onion with her head turned almost sideways, one eye squeezed shut, which worked about as well as it looked, meaning not at all. Theo laughed so hard he had to sit on the floor. Then she tried cutting the onion near the running faucet, because the recipe blog had mentioned it, and that helped a little, though she wasn't sure why and refused to guess.

For the last onion, she dug the swim goggles out of the pool bag by the back door. They left a red ring around her eyes and steamed up within a minute, but no tears. Theo watched her chop the entire onion, goggled and triumphant, while the onions softened in the pot and the kitchen began to smell like something good was actually happening.

"You look like a bug," Theo announced.

"A bug," Jade said, lifting the lid to drop in the potatoes, "who made dinner."

story:
The food bank smelled like cardboard and apples, and Tyler stood in the doorway with his gloves on before anyone told him where to go. A woman named Rosa handed him a clipboard and pointed to a folding table where three other volunteers were sorting donations from the weekend food drive. His job seemed simple: check the cans and boxes, put good items on the shelf, toss expired ones into the bin. He had signed up to conquer his Saturday boredom, but now that he was actually here, something on the table caught his eye.

A man at the end of the table, Mr. Duffy, held up a box of cereal and frowned at it. "One day past," he muttered, and dropped it toward the trash bin.

"Wait," Tyler said. "Isn't there a difference between a safety date and, like, a quality date?"

Mr. Duffy paused, the box hovering. "What do you mean?"

Tyler had read something on a poster in the lobby while he waited for Rosa, but he wanted to be sure. "I don't actually know. Can I check?" He walked back to the lobby, found the poster by the donation barrel, and read it twice. When he came back, he was almost running.

"In the United States, the USDA says a 'best if used by' date shows when a food will be at its best quality," Tyler said, holding up his phone where he'd snapped a picture of the poster. "It's not a food-safety date."

Mr. Duffy turned the cereal box over. "Huh. Look at that. It says best if used by. Not use by." He set the box back on the table instead of in the bin. "So where'd you learn that, kid?"

"I didn't, really. I just noticed the sign and wondered why there were two different phrases. Isn't that weird, that they'd bother printing different words?" Tyler picked up another box, this one crackers, and studied the date. "It's like a hidden rule. You can't see it just by looking at the shelf, but it changes what happens to every single item."

Rosa came over to see what the small crowd was about. Tyler explained the date thing, and she nodded slowly. "That's a good catch. We've been throwing out a lot of good food, then." She raised her voice to the whole room. "Everybody, from now on, check what kind of date it is before you toss it."

The sorting picked up speed after that. Tyler made a game of it, calling out "quality date" or "safety date" like a referee, and the other volunteers started racing him to spot the difference first. By noon the shelf was fuller than it had been all morning, and the trash bin held only half of what anyone expected. Was this how real scientists felt, he wondered, when some small phenomenon nobody else had noticed suddenly made a messy pile of things make sense?

The last donation bag held a dented can of peaches, robust and heavy in his hand, with no date he could find at all. Tyler turned it under the light, hunting along the seam.

"Found it yet?" Mr. Duffy called over.

"Not yet," Tyler said, and kept turning the can.

story:
Brayden lay on the couch with a box of tissues, a bowl of crackers, and three days of nothing but game shows. The flu had flattened him on Friday, right before his cousin Marcus's birthday party, which was tomorrow at noon. His mom had made a deal with him: if his fever stayed normal all morning, he could go. He wanted that more than anything, because Marcus had saved him the last slice of pizza every year since they were seven.

He was texting his friend Dev when a thought stopped his thumb mid-word. The sleepover. Dev had been there too, laughing and eating chips and winning every round of the racing game. Dev texted back that he was fine, but Brayden scrolled up in the group chat anyway. Saturday morning, two days ago, Dev had sent a single message: "ugh, think im getting the flu." Brayden stared at it, then counted on his fingers. Dev had been perfectly healthy at the sleepover on Friday night. Then, less than a full day later, he was sick.

Brayden sat up so fast the blanket slid to the floor. People with the flu could spread it starting about one day before they felt any symptoms. That meant Dev hadn't just caught it after the sleepover. He had probably been spreading it while they were all piled on the air mattress, sharing controllers and a bag of pretzels. Brayden's own fever had started Sunday, which was almost exactly one day after the sleepover. It lined up like a laser beam pointed straight at Friday night.

He had to test the idea. He messaged the other two boys from the sleepover. Ten minutes later, both had replied. Tyler: "fine so far." Owen: "my throat kinda hurts today." Owen had been the one who fell asleep with his head on Dev's shoulder during the movie. Brayden read the messages twice, letting the pattern digest. Two out of five boys sick within the same stretch of days, all of them exposed to the same person before that person knew he was sick.

Brayden walked to the kitchen where his mom was cutting fruit. "I figured out where I got it," he said. "Dev seemed totally fine at the sleepover, but you can spread the flu starting about one day before you even feel symptoms. So he was already contagious Friday night. Owen's getting sick too, and he was all over Dev." He took a breath. "So here's the thing. If I go to Marcus's party tomorrow, even with no fever, I might be doing the same thing Dev did."

His mom set down the knife and looked at him for a long moment. "That was an eloquent argument for a kid with a stuffy nose," she said. "Go call Marcus. Tell him the truth, and ask about that pizza."

Brayden dialed, and when Marcus picked up, he said, "I'm going to tell you something weird, and then I'm going to ask you a favor about pizza."

story:
Zoe stood at the boards with the sign-up sheet in her mitten, waiting for Priya to finish her lap. Their winter tournament allowed each team one pick from outside its regular roster, and they had argued about that pick all the way to the rink. "It has to be Dana," Priya said, skating over in a spray of ice. "She scores every single game. Her average is two goals a game." Zoe frowned at the clipboard. "Morgan's average is two a game too. I wrote them both down." Priya snorted. "Then it's a tie, so pick Dana. Everyone ranks Dana higher."

"But that's what's bugging me," Zoe said. "If they're tied on average, why does everyone say Dana is better? Nobody can actually see who's better. We only see the games." Priya rolled her eyes, but Zoe had already flipped her notebook to a page of tiny numbers. She had gone through the league website the night before, eating a nutritious dinner of toast with peanut butter while she copied down every game log. "Look. Dana: two goals, two goals, two, one, three, two, two. Same every night." She tapped the second column. "Morgan: five goals, zero, six, zero, zero, one, two. Same average. But Morgan swings between great and terrible games, and an average hides how spread out the results are." She said it out loud and then checked her math again, because it seemed too strange to be true. Two players, same average, completely different players.

"So which one do we want?" Priya said. Zoe proposed a test instead of an argument. "Next scrimmage, we put Morgan on our line and watch. If the spread thing is real, we should see it." At Saturday's scrimmage Morgan scored four goals in the first period, and Priya threw her arms around Zoe at the bench. In the second period Morgan missed an open net twice and passed to nobody, and Priya groaned. "That was a humiliation," she muttered, pulling her helmet straight. "Mine too," Morgan said, embarrassed, sitting down between them. Zoe slid the water bottle over. "You're still averaging two a game," she said. "That's what my notebook says, and my notebook has never lied to me yet."

By the end of the third period, Morgan had scored twice more, and the swing had shown up exactly as the numbers promised. Zoe did not gloat. Instead she asked Morgan one question: "Tournament games are single elimination. One bad game and we're out. Do you want to be our pick, knowing that?" Morgan thought about it, chipped the ice off her skate blade, and said, "Pick Dana. She never stops at two. I'll take a regular spot if you have one, and I'll work on the zeroes." Zoe crossed off one name and wrote the other.

On the walk to the parking lot, Priya bumped her shoulder. "You solved it with a notebook and toast." Zoe laughed. "The toast was the nutritious part. The numbers did the rest." Inside the rink, the Zamboni began its slow loops, and the noise of the fans would not cease until every last scrap of ice was smooth. Priya pointed at the driver's booth, where a new standings sheet had just gone up, team averages printed in tidy rows. "Look at that," she said. "All those games, squished into one number." Zoe grinned and tucked her notebook under her arm. "Not for long," she said, and turned back toward the doors.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Felix sat at the kitchen table wrapped in a quilt that smelled like the linen closet, staring at a bowl of chicken soup he had no intention of eating. His fever had spiked overnight, and now every joint in his body ached like he had run a marathon in his sleep. His little sister, Poppy, kept orbiting the table with her thermometer, pretending she was a nurse on television.

"Mom thinks we should wait until Saturday to call Dr. Okafor," she reported, tucking the thermometer into her doll's armpit. "Dad thinks you're going to turn into a zombie by Friday."

"I heard that," Mom called from the stove. She stirred something and sighed. "His fever is 102, but it might break on its own. The office is always packed on Thursdays."

Felix pushed the soup an inch away, then pulled it back, then pushed it away again, like the bowl itself was making the decision. His brain felt like wet sand, but something was nagging at him, a memory from a pamphlet he had read in Dr. Okafor's waiting room back in September, mostly because the magazine rack had nothing but golf catalogs. He tried to reconstruct it. The pamphlet had said something about flu medicine, the kind you get with a prescription, and a deadline. Two days. The medicine worked best if you started it within two days after symptoms began.

He counted backward on his fingers, which took longer than it should have. "Mom. When did I start feeling bad?"

"Tuesday night, sweetie. You were shivering during dinner."

"So the clock started Tuesday." He held up two fingers. "Two days. That's my window. If we wait until Saturday, I miss it, and the medicine won't do much." He slid the soup toward her like a lawyer presenting evidence. "Calling today isn't arbitrary. It's the rule."

Mom tapped the spoon against the pot. Poppy whispered "zombie" in a spooky voice.

"You read that somewhere?" Mom asked.

"Waiting room pamphlet. Golf rack, remember."

She laughed, wiped her hands on the towel, and picked up her phone. While she was on hold, Felix took one bite of soup and, to his own surprise, kept going. When Mom hung up, she said the nurse agreed completely and they could come at three.

At the clinic, Dr. Okafor wrote the prescription and said, "Good timing. This antiviral works best when it's started within two days of your first symptoms, so you caught it just right."

"Did you hear that, Poppy?" Felix said weakly from the exam table. "Your almost-zombie brother caught it just right."

On the drive home, he leaned against the window and decided that being right was a kind of currency in their family, worth at least one extra hour of video games. He planned to spend it the moment his hands stopped aching.

Then Poppy leaned over from her booster seat and pressed the thermometer into his ear. It beeped. "Ninety-eight point six," she announced. "My medicine worked. That'll be five dollars."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The lights went out just as Nora was finishing her homework, and the whole house sank into a blue evening dimness. She found her way to the back door and stepped onto the porch, where her older brother Dev was already standing with a flashlight, shining it at the empty birdbath as if it might explain things. Their little brother Milo was in the kitchen, and Nora could hear the refrigerator door swing open, then shut, then open again.

"Milo, stop that," she called through the screen door. "You're letting the cold out."

"I want the yogurt," his voice drifted back. "I can't find it in the dark."

Nora went inside and held the flashlight while Milo rummaged, but the beam wobbled and he moved containers aside, and she felt the cool air spilling past her ankles like water from a cracked cup. She remembered a poster from the school cafeteria, the one she'd read while waiting in the pizza line: according to the USDA, a fridge keeps food safely cold for about four hours in a power cut, as long as the door stays closed. Four hours, if it stayed shut. Milo was spending those hours a few seconds at a time.

"We get one open," Dev said from the doorway, having apparently been thinking the same thing. "Everybody decide first, then we open it once, grab everything, and shut it for good."

Milo looked ready to argue, but then his lower lip trembled and he sat down on the cold tile. Nora crouched beside him and tried to console him, saying they'd have a yogurt picnic as soon as they planned it right, and after a moment he wiped his nose on his sleeve and agreed. They made their list on the porch by flashlight: yogurt, the leftover noodles, the milk, the cheese, the orange juice Milo pretended not to want. They stacked it all in a cooler from the garage, next to the porous old cinder block that their father used as a doorstop, and then they sat on the steps eating cold noodles with forks, listening to crickets.

The power came back at half past nine, humming through the porch light and glowing yellow against the dusk. Dev stood up, stretched, and opened the refrigerator to put things away, and every bulb inside blazed on cheerfully. Nora laughed so hard she nearly dropped her fork, because the fridge had come back to life precisely when they no longer needed to keep it closed.

"Four hours of careful planning," Dev said, "wasted on ten minutes."

"Get me the yogurt," Milo announced from the steps. "I've decided."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
story:
Ariana counted the steps from the cabin to the dock, because if she knew exactly how far the lake was, maybe it would stop feeling like the edge of a map. Camp Wanaset claimed to be the most prestigious canoe camp in the county, and the banners everywhere said so, and her older brother had spent two summers here winning the paddle trophy that sat in the lodge. Ariana had never been away from home before, and today was the day every new camper got in a canoe for the first time.

"New campers, you're with me," said Kaya, who was fourteen and the tutor for beginners, meaning she took them out on the water every morning. Kaya wanted that trophy more than anything, and she kept glancing at the older campers racing near the far shore. "We paddle after lunch. Nobody flips my group."

At the dock, a boy named Dex went first. He stepped onto the edge of the canoe instead of the middle, and the whole boat lurched sideways under him. He grabbed the gunwale, the canoe wobbled again, and Kaya hauled him back onto the dock before he went in. "You're not getting in like that," she said. Dex's face went red, and he muttered something about quitting, because he had told everyone at breakfast he would catch the biggest fish in the lake from a canoe, and now he couldn't even sit down in one.

Ariana watched the older campers next. Every single one of them stepped into the middle of the canoe, and kept low, knees bent, gear centered between them. Nobody had said anything about it. They just did it, like it was a rule written somewhere she hadn't been shown. She looked at Dex wobbling on the dock and made a quiet guess: the boats tipped when weight went onto the side, and stayed calm when weight sat low and centered in the middle.

"Me next," she said. She stepped straight into the middle of the canoe, crouched, and slid onto the seat. The boat barely moved. Dex stared at her.

"How'd you do that?"

"Watch." She nodded at the older campers. "They all get in the same way." Dex tried again, stepping into the middle, low and slow, and this time the canoe held steady under him. He gripped his paddle and grinned.

Later, they would transport their gear across the lake to the fishing spot, and the whole camp would see two first-timers paddling out flat and calm. For now Kaya pushed them off from the dock and jumped into her own boat, eyes already on the far shore.

"Race you to the reeds," Dex called, and dug his paddle in.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Katherine had exactly one class period to finish her shaded sphere for the art show, and her pencil was betraying her. The highlight kept turning gray no matter how lightly she touched the paper. Across the table, Marcus held up two pencils that looked identical, both yellow, both freshly sharpened. "Why does this one draw so dark and this one barely shows up?" he asked. "They're the same size. It's like one of them is lazy."

Katherine took both pencils and scribbled a quick swatch on scrap paper. One left a rich, velvety black; the other left a mark so faint it looked like a ghost of a pencil. She turned them near the window and noticed small letters on each one. The dark one said 4B. The pale one said 4H. "They're not the same kind," she said. "The letters are different." Marcus leaned over her shoulder, nearly knocking her eraser off the table, and she caught it before it rolled away.

"My grandpa has a whole coffee can of these at his house," Katherine said, turning the pencils over. "He told me once what the letters mean, but I forgot most of it." She remembered one part, though, a sentence he'd said while she sat at his kitchen table drawing horses: pencil cores aren't just one thing, they're graphite powder mixed with clay. She frowned at the pale pencil. "So if more clay makes a harder pencil that leaves lighter marks, then this 4H one must have more clay in it than the 4B."

"Test it," Marcus said, always ready for anything that sounded even slightly like science class. Katherine pressed down hard with the 4H, then feather-light with the 4B. Even under pressure, the hard pencil stayed pale, and even with the gentlest touch, the soft one smudged dark. "It's backwards from what you'd expect," she said. "The harder one gives you less." Marcus squinted at his own drawing. "So that's why my clouds look like storm clouds. I've been using the dark one for everything."

He looked so defeated that Katherine slid her 4H across the table to him. "Try this for the light parts. And press less with the dark one for the middle." She watched him shade a cloud so fluffy it looked ready to float off his page, and he grinned like he'd invented weather.

For her sphere's highlight, she finally understood what to do. Instead of pressing the dark pencil lighter and lighter, which only eroded the paper's tooth into a shiny smudge, she used the hard pencil with its faint, pale mark, letting the white of the page glow through at the very top. Her shading curved around the sphere now, giving it real perspective, the way Mr. Okafor kept saying, like it existed in actual space and not just flat on the desk. At the end of class he held up her sphere as an example, calling it "a thoroughly contemporary take on a classic exercise," which made Marcus whisper, "He just means it looks cool."

Katherine wrote 4H on the back of her scrap paper and tucked it in her pocket, next to two pencils she'd decided to keep forever. "Grandpa's going to be proud," she said. "That thing you figured out," Marcus said, gathering his cloud drawing, "can you teach it to my little sister? Her cat drawings look like they got caught in a rainstorm." Katherine laughed. "Bring her a 4H," she said, "and tell her the pale pencil is her best friend."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Mila had made Grandma Rosa's snickerdoodles three times this winter, and every batch came out the same: dry in the middle, puffy like little cakes instead of flat and chewy. She stood at the counter with the recipe card propped against the flour canister, reading it again. Her dad's voice drifted in from the hallway, where he was on the phone with her uncle about the wind turbine they were helping install at the school, and she half listened while she puzzled over the card. The recipe said two and a quarter cups of flour, the same as always. She hadn't changed anything.

Or maybe she had. She thought about how she measured. She dipped the measuring cup straight into the bag, the way she always had, and the flour came up in a dense block that she leveled with a knife. She remembered Grandma Rosa weighing her flour on the little silver scale instead, and how she used to transmit recipes by letter, with weights written beside the cups. Grandma had texted her the gram amounts last week: two hundred and seventy grams for two and a quarter cups. Mila had never bothered with them. Cups were faster.

She pulled the scale from the top shelf and set the bowl on it, pressing tare until the numbers cleared. Then she scooped a cup of flour the way she always did, packed and leveled, and poured it in. The scale read one hundred and sixty grams, not one hundred and twenty. She frowned and did the next cup. One hundred and fifty-five. She measured the last quarter cup and then checked the total: over three hundred and forty grams. Almost eighty grams more than the recipe meant. Eighty grams was like adding a whole extra half cup that nobody asked for.

"Whoa," her little brother Theo said, appearing at her elbow with his synthetic vanilla-spiked hot chocolate, which Mom had finally bought after the real vanilla bottle ran dry. "Why's the number so big?" Mila tapped the bag of flour. "Scooping straight from the bag packs it down, so a cup holds way more than the recipe wants. That's why they're coming out like little cakes." She dumped the flour back, spooned it gently into the cup, leveled it, and weighed again. One hundred and twenty-five grams. Closer. She did the rest the same way, watching the numbers climb toward two hundred and seventy exactly.

The dough felt different under her hands, softer and slacker, and it spread on the pan in fat rounds instead of sitting stiff. When the timer buzzed, the cookies came out golden with crackled tops, and when she broke one in half it pulled apart in strings. Theo took one before it was even cool. "These are the real ones," he said through a full mouth. Mila set two aside on the good plate and took out her phone to text Grandma Rosa a picture. She typed, "You were right, I weighed the flour," and pressed send. Then she ate the broken cookie standing up, right there beside the warm oven.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
story:
The casseroles kept arriving like a currency nobody had asked for, dish after dish stacking up on Grandma's old kitchen table, and Christopher hadn't touched a bite of any of them. It had been six days since Grandpa died, and in those six days Christopher had slept maybe two hours a night, maybe less. His legs felt hollow. He pushed a fork through the lasagna and watched the cheese go cold.

"You look terrible," his cousin Marcus said, cornering him by the punch bowl.

"Thanks."

"No, I mean it. Are you sick?" Marcus leaned closer. "If you're getting the flu the day before the funeral, my mom will lose her mind. She's already losing it."

That was the thing, the worry that had been circling him all week like a fly he couldn't swat. Because it wasn't just the sleeping. It was that food made his throat close. It was that his hands shook carrying the mail. He had started building a list in his head: mono, or something worse, something they'd catch too late, and he'd be in a hospital bed while everyone was already standing at a grave. Tomorrow. The funeral was tomorrow at ten, and he was supposed to read the card he'd written, and his body was falling apart on a schedule.

He tried an experiment that afternoon. He went into the den where his dad was sorting Grandpa's old photographs, and he said, straight out, "Dad, are you sleeping?"

His dad didn't look up. "Couple hours a night. Maybe."

"Are you eating?"

Dad finally turned. "Your aunt made me finish half a sandwich today. First real thing since Sunday." He squinted at Christopher. "Why?"

Christopher pulled a chair over. "My hands shake. My stomach's wrong. I thought maybe I was getting sick, but." He stopped. "You sleep two hours. You eat half a sandwich. And Aunt Terri looks the same way. And Marcus's mom was awake at three, I heard her in the kitchen."

Dad set down the photo he was holding, one of Grandpa holding a fish the size of a canoe paddle. "Grief doesn't just mess with your feelings," he said quietly. "It can get into your body too. Tiredness, sleep going bad, appetite going strange. It happens."

"So I'm not sick."

"You're not sick." Dad rubbed his eyes. "It's just grief, invading everything, the whole system."

Christopher sat with that. Then he asked about the second part of his test, the part that actually scared him. "Then how do I read the card tomorrow if I'm like this?"

"You eat something small tonight. You sleep as much as your body lets you. That's the fix. Not a radical one, just a boring one."

At the evening meal, in front of everybody, Christopher took a piece of bread and ate it slowly, bite by bite, while his aunts pretended not to watch. It went down. It stayed down. He went to bed at nine and lay in the dark listening to his grandmother's clock tick in the hallway, and he slept four whole hours, which felt like an ocean.

In the morning he put on the gray shirt his mom had laid out and found the card in his jacket pocket where he'd left it. At the funeral home, when the pastor nodded to him, Christopher stood up. His hands were steadier than they'd been all week. He unfolded the card, looked out at the folding chairs and the flowers and his father's tired face, and began, "My grandpa taught me to fish."

"Speak up, buddy," his dad called softly.

Christopher lifted his chin and said it again, louder, to the whole room.
