activity: trying out for a school sports team
story:
The zamboni had just finished its slow lap, and the ice smelled like cold pennies and burnt rubber when Keira laced her skates at the boards. Day one of hockey tryouts, and forty girls were racing lines under the whir of the fans. Coach Reyes skated the perimeter to supervise each drill, whistle in her teeth, stopwatch in her glove.

Keira went all out. She sprinted the lengths, slammed through the checking drill, and won every board battle along the wall. By the end of practice her legs were trembling, but she felt great, and Marisol, her best friend and her rival for the last forward spot, felt great too. They compared notes in the locker room, dripping and laughing. "Tomorrow we do it all again," Marisol said, pulling her pads off. "I feel like a laser. Nothing's slowing me down."

Day two, Marisol hobbled in like a rusty robot. She gripped the rail in the lobby, wincing at each stair, and stared at her own legs as if they'd betrayed her overnight. "I was fine last night," she groaned. "I even did extra jumps in my driveway." Keira frowned. Her own thighs ached too, worse than yesterday, which was strange. If skating had hurt them, the hurt should have shown up right away, not a full day later, like a bill arriving in the mail. Her older brother had once complained he couldn't sit down for three days after his first squat workout, fine the first evening and destroyed on day two. Keira had filed it away as weird. Now she watched Marisol lower herself onto the bench and thought, this is the same thing.

She tested the idea on her own body. Her hamstrings, which she'd stretched gently that morning, ached but worked. Her quads, which she'd hammered, were stiff as boards. So the pain arrived late, somewhere between a day and three days after, and it picked whatever muscles had been pushed hardest. She said it out loud, grinning. "Delayed onset muscle soreness. My brother calls it DOMS." Marisol squinted. "So yesterday's practice is only hitting me now?" "Now through maybe three days from now," Keira said.

Then came the twist Keira hadn't planned. Coach Reyes split them into scrimmage lines and put Marisol on defense, not because she was slow but because her legs couldn't take forward sprinting today. Keira got Marisol's spot at wing, and she hated how she got it. Between periods she skated over. "You should have it when you're whole," she told her. "Coach, can we rerun this Friday?" Reyes raised an eyebrow, then nodded once.

Friday, both girls fresh-legged, raced the length of the ice side by side, sticks clattering, ice chips flying like glass. "Whatever happens," Marisol panted, "remind me never to do driveway jumps after day one again." Keira laughed and leaned into the turn.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
story:
Colton sat on the crinkly paper of the exam table with his elbows on his knees, staring at the two dark half-moons under his arms. They had shown up halfway through morning announcements, and PJ Torres had announced them to half the hallway like it was breaking news. Now Dr. Marsh was tapping the screen, and Colton waited for his chance.

"Growing bodies sweat more," Dr. Marsh said. "It's normal." She handed him a sample card. "What matters is what you buy. Check the label."

That was it. No cure, no pill. In the waiting room, Mom flipped through a magazine while Colton's little brother narrated the fish tank, and Colton turned the sample card over and over. Whatever the doctor knew, she had left the actual answer for him to find.

The drugstore was two doors down. Colton stood in the deodorant aisle while his brother wandered toward the candy, and he read labels like his life depended on it, because tryouts were Thursday and the gym had no air conditioning. Two sticks sat side by side. One said antiperspirant, one said deodorant. He had always thought they were just two words for the same thing, but the fine print did not agree. The antiperspirant box said it reduces sweating by temporarily plugging sweat ducts. He read it twice, then turned to the other. That one never mentioned stopping sweat at all, only odor, reducing it or covering the smell.

"Those are opposites, basically," Colton said to his brother, who had drifted back with a pack of gum. "Antiperspirant stops the wet. Deodorant only handles the stink."

"So get the wet one," his brother said, already bored.

It was that simple, and it wasn't. Colton thought about PJ and the hallway jury that had laughed at his shirt. The antiperspirant stopped the actual sweating, which was the whole problem. The deodorant would just put perfume on top of it. His old stick, he realized, had been a deodorant all along, which explained a lot about the last month. Trying to fix it by layering on three swipes every morning had been reckless; it had done nothing but waste time.

He took the antiperspirant to the register with his own five dollars. Thursday afternoon, in the hot gym, he took his shot, ran the lines, raised his hand for the pass, and kept his arms up on purpose. Afterward, he pulled his shirt away from his body and looked. Dry. He walked past PJ on the way to the water fountain and lifted his arm to wipe his forehead.

"Nice tryout," PJ said.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
story:
Megan slid her poster board under the lab table and pulled out the two jars she had brought from home. One had held soup left open on the counter for a week, and it was now cloudy and streaked with green fuzz. The other had been sealed since the day she made it, and it looked almost the same as fresh. Her science fair project was due in three days, and she still could not answer the question her little brother had accused her of dodging: "If germs are everywhere in the air, why didn't the sealed jar go bad?"

In the empty science classroom after school, she laid the jars side by side and tapped the sealed lid. Something invisible was the problem, and she could not watch it happen. What she needed was a testable guess, something she could check with an experiment instead of just arguing about it. In class they had called that kind of guess a hypothesis, and Mr. Reyes kept saying a good one could either win or lose, as long as it could lose. "The soup went bad because something from the air got in," she wrote in her notebook. "If I let air in but keep the dust out, the soup should stay clean."

She was on her second try at bending glass tubing over the burner when Marcus from her class wandered in to grab his backpack. "You're going to set off the alarm, being that reckless with a flame," he said, but he stayed to watch. She had drawn a diagram from the old science book on the shelf, the one with the picture of swan-shaped flasks. She told him what the caption said while she worked the glass into a long S-shaped curve. "Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long S-shaped necks, and the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck." Marcus leaned over her shoulder. "So the neck is the whole trick?"

"It's my whole protagonist," Megan said, pointing her pen at the curve in the glass. "The jar that went bad is just the villain." She filled her homemade flask with broth, boiled it on the hot plate until steam rolled off, and set it beside an open jar of the same broth as her control. Then she labeled both and carried them to the windowsill, where they would sit for the next two days.

On Thursday she almost ran to the classroom. The open jar had gone cloudy and sour-smelling, and she held her breath as she lifted the flask with the curved neck. The broth inside was clear, no fuzz, no film on the glass. The bend had done its job while the open mouth had let trouble straight in. Marcus looked over the jars, then at her notebook, where she had written one last line and underlined it twice: hypothesis supported.

Mr. Reyes stopped at her table on his way past the windowsill, picked up the flask, and turned it in the light. Megan stood there grinning, waiting for the question she finally knew how to answer. "So," he said, "tell me why this one is still clean."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
story:
Brooke had promised the science fair committee a volcano, and now she regretted it, because everyone built volcanoes, and hers was going to look exactly like the one Marcus Reyes was building two lab tables away.

"You know why they erupt, right?" Marcus said, holding up his vinegar bottle like a trophy. "Baking soda plus vinegar. The baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, the vinegar is acetic acid, and together they make carbon dioxide gas. That's what pushes everything out. Everybody knows that."

"Everybody also builds the same cone out of papier-mâché," Brooke said. She looked down at her own cone, gray and lumpy, and decided she'd rather lose than present a third identical volcano. If the gas did the pushing, then the amount of gas ought to matter, which meant the amount of vinegar ought to matter, and nobody ever checked. She could test it. Three bottles, three different amounts, same baking soda each time, and a ruler taped to a wall behind the volcano to measure how high each eruption reached.

Mr. Okafor wandered past and did not offer help, which was his way of saying he trusted them, or possibly that he was being negligent about supervising the vinegar supply. Either way, Brooke got to work. The first trial, a small splash of vinegar, produced a sad burp that barely reached ten centimeters. The second, half a bottle, shot foam past the thirty-centimeter mark and splattered Marcus's notebook.

"Hey. That stuff hindered my data," Marcus said, wiping off his page.

"Then maybe you should collect some," Brooke said, and to her surprise, he came over. His project, it turned out, was just a volcano with red food coloring, no measurements at all, and the fair was in two days. He had an obligation to his partner too, which he had been ignoring.

They ran six trials together, trading the jobs of pouring and reading the ruler. More vinegar meant a taller eruption every single time, and the numbers lined up so neatly that Brooke wrote them twice to be sure. Marcus copied the last column into his notebook, then looked at his plain red cone the way you look at a sandwich next to a banquet.

"We're combining projects," he announced. "Your measurements, my cone. Mine has better paint."

Brooke considered arguing, but his cone did have better paint. "Fine," she said. "But I'm the one who says how much vinegar goes in the bottle."

"Deal," said Marcus, and handed her the ruler.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Mathis had been camped on the couch for three days, surrounded by crumpled tissues, a thermometer, and half a glass of orange juice he kept forgetting about. The flu was finally loosening its grip, but his nose still felt like a leaky faucet. His little sister Nadia wandered in, holding her toothbrush, and stood at the edge of his blanket nest.

"Why do you keep telling me to use soap?" she said. "I rinsed my hands with water just now. They're clean. See?" She held them out like evidence.

Mathis squinted at her from under the blanket. "Water just slides off the virus," he said. "Soap breaks apart the fatty outer layer that surrounds flu viruses. That's why washing with soap gets rid of them better than rinsing with water alone."

Nadia blinked. "The virus has a layer? Like a coat?"

"Kind of." He sat up, interested despite himself. "Think of it like grease on a pan. You can rinse a greasy pan forever and it stays greasy. Add soap and it comes apart." He paused. "At least, that's what I think happens. Let me check." He grabbed his phone from the armrest, typed with one thumb, and scrolled. "Huh. Yeah. That's the consensus. Every source says the same thing."

"So my hands are still covered in viruses?" Nadia stared at her palms like they'd betrayed her.

"Probably. I've been sneezing on every doorknob in this house for three days." Mathis pushed the blanket back. "Come on. Let's do an experiment."

In the kitchen, he found the olive oil and a dinner plate. He poured a thin puddle of oil onto the plate. "Pretend this oil is the fatty layer. Dip your finger in water and try to wipe it off." Nadia swiped at the oil. It smeared and stayed, a slick rainbow smear across the white plate.

"Now try with soap." She lathered her finger and dragged it through. The oil broke apart and lifted away, clinging to the foam in little beads. She did it again, and again, watching the plate go clean.

"So the virus just... falls apart?" she said.

"That's the idea. Its coat gets broken up." Mathis turned the plate under the tap, watching the last oily streaks vanish. It was strange to think about, all those invisible things on doorknobs and hands, held together by something so delicate. What else was floating around that nobody could see?

Nadia washed her hands at the sink, properly this time, humming while she scrubbed. Then she pointed at Mathis. "You should wash too. You're the one who's sick."

He held up his hands in surrender and headed for the bathroom. "Fine," he called over his shoulder. "But nobody touches my orange juice."

She was still thinking about what she had said in the hallway that morning: that most students at their school walked to school. Marcus had laughed and called it a wild guess, and she had walked away with her ears burning.

Now Mr. Okafor was writing two words on the board: opinion and claim. He would not say much, only that the class would spend the period deciding which of the statements on his desk belonged in each column. Samantha slid her bean tray aside and leaned forward.

"Most students at our school walk to school," Mr. Okafor read aloud. "Opinion or claim?"

"Opinion," said Priya. "Nobody knows that."

"But you could find out," Samantha said, before she could stop herself. "You could ask everybody. Like a survey."

Marcus turned around in his seat. "Nobody has asked everybody."

"So?" Samantha's heart was beating fast. "It can still be checkable even if nobody has checked it yet. If we took a survey, we'd know."

The room went quiet. Mr. Okafor tapped the board. "Could we actually do that?"

"We could count," Priya said slowly. "At the doors, in the morning. Walkers, bus riders, car riders."

They planned it right there. On Tuesday, Samantha stood at the front doors with a clipboard, making a tally mark for every student who arrived on foot. Priya took the side doors and Marcus, who had volunteered before Samantha could ask him, took the gym entrance. By first bell Samantha's fingers were cold and her column of tally marks ran down the whole page.

They typed the numbers into the classroom database, which Mr. Okafor kept for experiments, and the bar chart appeared on the screen. Walkers were the tallest bar. Not by much, though, and the bus bar was close behind. Samantha stared at it, remembering how certain she had sounded in the hallway, how sure. She had been right, mostly, and somehow that felt less like winning than she had expected.

"Well?" Marcus said, leaning over her shoulder at the screen. "Were you right or not?"

"Close enough that it's probable I'd be right again next time," Samantha said. "But I'd have to count again to know for sure."

Marcus grinned and shook the clipboard at her. "Same time Thursday?"

The bus smelled like wet raincoats and old vinyl, and Cameron had the letter folded in his back pocket, which meant he'd read it eleven times since breakfast. Mr. Reyes had clipped it from the local paper and dropped it on Cameron's desk with a shrug, saying only, "Thought you'd want this, since you're at that park every Saturday." The letter said the new skate park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste, and Cameron's stomach had been clenched ever since.

He slid into the seat across from Dana, who was nursing a cold and sniffling into a tissue. "Don't breathe on me," she said. "My mom says this virus is going around the whole school." Cameron held his breath for three seconds out of politeness, then gave up. He unfolded the letter and smoothed it on his knee.

"Read this," he said. Dana read it. Behind them, Marcus leaned over the seat, because Marcus leaned over every seat on the bus, that was practically his job.

"Two million dollars," Marcus said. "That's a lie. My uncle works for the city. It was two million." Cameron frowned at the paper. If the number was right, then that part of the letter wasn't a lie at all. You could look it up. You could call the city office, or find the budget online, and the number would either be true or it wouldn't. Dana blew her nose and said, "So the letter's true, then?"

"No," Cameron said slowly. "Not all of it." He read the last words again. A waste. That was the part that had been buzzing in his head since breakfast like a fly against a window. His little sister had asked at dinner whether the park really was a waste, and their dad had said that was somebody's opinion, not a fact, but he'd said it fast and then gone back to his noodles, and Cameron hadn't gotten it until just now, on a bus that rattled over every pothole on Marsh Road.

"Here's the thing," he said, holding up the letter so both of them could see it. "The cost can be checked, but 'a waste' is an opinion." Dana squinted at him. "So?" Cameron tapped the paper. "So when Mr. Reyes asks us Monday about stuff like this, that's the whole trick. One sentence can have both in it. Like if I said the ocean, which covers most of Earth, is boring. The covering part you could check. The boring part is just me." Marcus drummed his fingers on the seat back. "So whoever wrote this could be right about the money and still be wrong about the park."

"Or right about the park and lying about the money," Dana said, and sneezed into her tissue.

The bus groaned around the corner by the field where the last endangered cranes nested each spring, and Cameron folded the letter along its old creases. He was already planning what he'd write back to the paper, something that started with the number and ended with Saturday morning, his board under his arm, the whole park loud with wheels and nobody complaining. "First thing Monday," he told them, "I'm asking Mr. Reyes if we can print both."

story:
Kate sat at the kitchen table with her laptop open, the cursor blinking in the To field of a new email. Her best friend Priya's surprise party was in two weeks, and Kate wanted to invite the whole science class, all twenty-six of them. The problem was that she only had about nine addresses of her own. The rest lived in a class list Mr. Okafor had sent out in September, and she remembered, vaguely, that his message had come to her with everyone else invisible somehow. She scrolled through her inbox until she found it, but when she opened his email, the To field showed only her own address. Nothing else. That was strange. If he had sent it to the whole class, where were the other names?

Her dad came in and set down a piece of paper on the counter, sighing at it. "Parking citation," he said. "I was four minutes over at the meter." He shook his head and poured coffee. Kate barely looked up. She clicked Reply on Mr. Okafor's message and studied it again. Maybe he had sent the same email twenty-six separate times? That seemed like a lot of work, but it would explain the empty field. She decided to test a smaller version of the idea. She opened a new email to Priya and typed a joke subject line, then noticed, below the To field, two more boxes: Cc and Bcc.

She typed her own address in To and Priya's address in Bcc, just to see, and sent the words "testing, ignore this." Her laptop was quiet except for the refrigerator hum and the soft tick of the wall clock. When the message arrived a second later, she opened it. It said To: Kate. Priya was nowhere on it. She forwarded that message to herself too, and Priya's address stayed invisible. So the Bcc field was the hidden cause, the rule that governed how Mr. Okafor had sent the list without showing anyone's address to anyone else.

She called Priya to check her thinking. "Did you get a weird test email from me?"

"Two of them," Priya said, laughing. Kate smiled; Priya's laugh was exactly her grandmother's, hereditary and unmistakable. "Why'd you send it like that?"

"Bcc," Kate said. "It stands for blind carbon copy. People in that field get the message, but nobody else can see their addresses." She said it out loud and felt it settle into place, like a key turning.

"So you can invite the class without sharing everyone's email with everyone else," Priya said.

"Exactly. Nobody's address gets passed around, and nobody sees who else is invited." Kate started pasting addresses into the Bcc field, one by one, twenty-six of them. Then she typed, in her cheerfully loud party voice, all capital letters and exclamation points, the kind of tone she would never use in a quiet note to her grandmother: SURPRISE PARTY FOR PRIYA!!! Then she deleted it, because Priya was on the phone and could hear her typing. She retyped it as a secret code instead: "Study group at my house, Saturday, bring your periodic table."

"Sounds boring," Priya said. "Perfect."

Kate hovered over Send and double-checked that the To field held her own address, and only hers, a single name standing guard over twenty-five secrets.

Brayden balanced the mixing bowl on the picnic table and checked the recipe again, though he had memorized it by now. Mom's birthday biscuits, the ones his grandfather used to make, and Brayden had promised the whole family a batch at tonight's backyard dinner. The garden behind him was lush after a week of rain, and the grill already smelled like charcoal, but the biscuits were his job alone.

He reached for the tin marked baking powder and tilted it. Empty. A few grains sifted out and that was all. The nearest store was a twenty-minute bike ride, and the potatoes needed watching on the grill, so riding away wasn't really an option. He stood there with the tin in his hand, feeling the old resentment from last summer rise up, the time he'd quit halfway through Grandpa's recipe book and Grandpa had quietly finished it himself. This year Brayden wanted to preserve that recipe, not lose it, and quitting twice felt like the same failure twice.

In the cupboard by the back door he found a box of baking soda and thought, close enough. He stirred it in, cut the dough, and set the tray on the grill's side shelf where the heat was gentle. Ten minutes later he lifted the lid and stared. The biscuits had gone flat and faintly bitter, nothing like the tall golden ones in the photo.

He sat down on the step and turned it over. The pancake batter Grandpa made used buttermilk, sour and tangy, and it always rose high. These biscuits used plain milk. Soda went in where buttermilk went in. Powder went in where nothing sour went in. Brayden stood up slowly. The box of baking soda needed something acidic in the batter to do its work. He grabbed his phone and read the label on a baking powder tin in a photo: it already contained both baking soda and a dry acid, which was why a recipe didn't need anything acidic for the batter to rise.

"Then I'll add the acid myself," he said out loud. He found lemon juice in the fridge, mixed a fresh batch with plain milk, soda, and a careful spoonful of juice, and slid the tray back onto the warm shelf. His little sister wandered over and peeked under the foil.

"Smell like Grandpa's," she said.

"Better," Brayden said, and lifted the lid on eight tall, golden biscuits.

Elliot's little sister had been coughing for three nights, and his mother had sent him to the pharmacy on Marsh Street with twenty dollars and one instruction: bring back something that actually worked. He stood in the cold-and-flu aisle between two boxes. The first box, bright orange, had a photograph of a smiling man and the words "I felt better in one day!" printed across the top. The second box, plain white, said "Tested in a study of 420 adults." Elliot turned both boxes over in his hands. Forty-two dollars, though. Way over budget. There was a third option, a store brand for eight dollars with no photograph and no study, just a list of ingredients.

A man in a rain jacket was standing beside him, holding a tube of sunscreen. "Get the orange one," the man said. "That stuff saved me in February. One dose and I was a new person."

"Thanks," Elliot said, but he didn't reach for the orange box. One person. One February. He put the eight-dollar store brand in his basket anyway, because it had the same ingredients as the white one, which he'd checked twice, letter by letter.

At the counter, he counted his money and found he could also afford the sunscreen, which his mother had asked for if there was anything left. The pharmacist, a woman with reading glasses on a chain, rang it up. "Good timing on this," she said. "We ran out all week. Our supplier tested it on volunteers who live right near the equator, where the sun is strongest. They couldn't keep it on the shelf down there."

Elliot looked at the tube. "How many volunteers?"

"About three hundred, the label says." She turned the tube so he could see the small print. "Big studies like that, they're more reliable than one person swearing by something. With enough people, the flukes just even out."

"That's what I was thinking," Elliot said, and he meant it, though he hadn't been able to articulate it that clearly in the aisle. He thought of the man in the rain jacket, one person, one February. He thought of the smiling face on the orange box. Then he thought of 420 adults, all coughing, all taking the same white pills, most of them getting better. Maybe some of them hadn't. But with that many people, the ones who would have recovered anyway and the ones who never improved wouldn't be able to hide the truth. His own idea felt more robust suddenly, less like a guess.

He was almost out the door when he noticed a shelf of cough drops with a sign: "Voted Best by Our Customers." Underneath, in smaller letters, it said "Based on a survey of 350 shoppers." Three hundred fifty people. He imagined his three friends from science class voting on something, all agreeing, and how that could still be wrong. This was different. He picked up a bag of the honey-lemon drops and added them to his basket.

At home, his sister took the syrup without complaint, and the drops turned out to be the real prize. She held one up and studied it like a tiny amber stone.

"Where'd you get these?" she asked.

"The pharmacy," Elliot said. "A lot of people picked them."

Christopher sat two rows behind Marcus and refused to look at him, which was hard, because Mr. Delgado had just asked the class to nominate a partner for the history project. Marcus raised his hand and pointed at Priya. He did not even glance back.

At lunch Christopher didn't sit with him, and at afternoon study hall he wrote in his notebook: Marcus picked Priya, so Marcus is done with me. But the sentence bothered him. Priya had the best notes in the class, and Marcus needed a good grade to stay on the basketball team. Maybe Marcus hadn't picked her over him at all. Maybe he had just picked a good partner. Christopher couldn't see inside Marcus's head, but he could test one idea. He wrote a second line: If I tell him what I think happened, and repeat back what he says, I'll know if he's mad or just busy.

In English the next morning, their teacher mentioned that the term "active listening" was introduced by the psychologists Carl Rogers and Richard Farson in 1957. It means trying to understand the speaker's point of view, Christopher thought, often by repeating their meaning back in your own words. He copied the sentence down, then circled it twice.

He caught Marcus by the lockers after the last bell. "You could've asked me to be your partner," Christopher said. "I was going to, but you skipped lunch on Tuesday and I thought you were avoiding me, so I panicked," Marcus said. "So you felt I was already dumping you as a friend," Christopher said, repeating the meaning back. Marcus's shoulders dropped about two inches. "Yeah. Exactly that."

Christopher had been sure Marcus had chosen Priya because Priya was cooler, or because their friendship was somehow over, and now he could feel that certainty cracking apart. It was strange how a thing he couldn't see, the reason behind one raised hand, could look so dark from two rows back and so ordinary up close. "Mr. Delgado says we can have groups of three," Marcus said. "Priya's cool with it. We're doing descendants of local founders, and apparently one of them had a controversial past, some land dispute thing." "I'm in," Christopher said. "But I pick where we work. My house. Your mom's dog ate my homework once." Marcus laughed and shoved his locker shut. "Deal," he said, and they walked out together into the cold.

story:
Emilie spread the poster board across two folding tables at the family reunion, her markers lined up like tools. Her friend Priya's sign-language club needed a banner for the school fair, and Emilie had promised it for Monday. Across the top, in fat blue letters, she had written: PRIDE IN deaf CULTURE. Her cousin Marco leaned over her shoulder, arms crossed, frowning at the small d.

"You got that wrong," he signed, his hands quick and sharp. His mother, Aunt Rena, translated from the lawn chair beside the table. "He says the D should be capital."

"Since when does deaf get a capital letter?" Emilie signed back, slowly, because her signing was still clunky. Marco snorted and wandered off toward the volleyball game, leaving her with the poster and the problem.

She remembered the club's first meeting in September, how Priya had stood at the whiteboard and said her grandmother was deaf and that the club would learn her language. Nobody had mentioned capitals then. Emilie had assumed deaf was like tall or tired, just a description. But Marco had grown up with two Deaf parents. If he was fussy about one letter, the letter meant something, though she could not see what. The rule was invisible; she needed someone to show her where it lived.

She found Marco's mother by the dessert table, filling a plate with lemon bars. "Aunt Rena, why does Marco care about the capital D?"

"Because of something from 1972," Aunt Rena said. "A linguist, James Woodward, proposed writing Deaf with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase deaf for the hearing condition itself." She tapped the plate. "Two different things, one spelling apart."

Emilie turned that over while Aunt Rena went back for a second lemon bar. Capital D for the people, the language, the belonging. Small d for the ears. Priya's club was about people and language, so it was Deaf. Marco wasn't being picky; he was being exact, the way Grandpa was exact about calling himself an artisan instead of a hobbyist woodworker, because the word carried who he was.

Back at the table, Emilie tested the rule on every line of the poster. Deaf culture, capital. When the club text mentioned Priya's grandmother losing her hearing, that part was deaf, lowercase, the condition. She filled in the big D with red marker, pressing hard, then held the poster up across the yard so Marco could see it.

He jogged over, studied it, and gave her a slow thumbs-up. "Better," he signed. Then he pointed at her blank bottom margin and grinned. "Now make it beautiful."

"Give me those yellow markers," Emilie said. "And somebody keep Uncle Vic away from the table. Last year he signed my name on my own birthday banner and I was gullible enough to hang it up."

Marco laughed, a sound like two hands clapping, and tossed her the yellow.
